title: Magic: The Gathering Reality Fracture Review, Part 1 of 4 - The Mechanics
content:
At the crossroads of Jace’s rampant egomania and ‘what if I drew a fucked up, evil version of the Hamburger Helper’ lies Reality Fracture, Magic’s newest set. This is the first Planeswalkers-matter set since 2019’s War of the Spark, or should we say Planeswalker, singular, as Jace is the set’s focal point. Reality Fracture is filled with powerful cards and their alternate universe counterparts, offering both novel mechanical takes on beloved characters, and imaginative ‘what-if’ scenarios for Vorthoses. To that end, this set is built for pick-2 draft, with both versions of many characters appearing alongside one another in the same pack. After a couple of middling releases, this set is probably the most powerful since Avatar, and we expect a host of multi-format staples to solidify once players get their hands on Reality Fracture. This week, we’re covering the set’s mechanics, focusing on two new types of token

Reality Fracture officially releases to tabletop on October 2nd, and on Magic: The Gathering Arena on September 29th.

New Mechanics

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Empower (Jace)

This is a new spin on Amass, but instead of a growing Army, you’re afforded a Jace token with the appropriate Loyalty counters. This is a mechanically intricate action, with niche cases like being able to rapidly ultimate a ‘normal’ Jace that’s been turned into a token, or borrow the abilities of Planeswalkers like Kasmina, Enigma Sage. Unlike the original Amass, the designers left themselves room to create different versions of Empower in future sets, now that Jace has left the narrative. These would create different tokens, but still retain the timing and counter placement of the core Empower mechanic.

Saffgor: In its simplest form, you can evaluate all instances of Empower of 2 or less as ‘Surveil 1-ish’, and 3+ as ‘Draw 1 card-ish’, because the Jace token can do so much more if it’s allowed to. Against decks worried about the value game, like all Planeswalkers he effectively gains you life, and in eternal formats Reality Scramble flips him into whatever other one Planeswalker you have in your Library. It’s shocking how many niche interactions are propelled by token Planeswalkers arriving via non-Planeswalker cards, and I even got a chance to cover a new 2-card combo enabled by Empower Jace in last week’s Puzzlebox. One last thing—that Surveil mode is usually available every turn he persists, and this helps colors which otherwise lack the ability to fill the yard (Red & White, mostly) to start putting things in the bin. For decks like my beloved Gau, Feral Youth or White reanimator by way of Queen of Dale, this is a godsend.

BPhillipYork: Empower Jace is kind of weird. Obviously he's very front and center in this set, and the ability to have random planeswalkers popping into play is an interesting one with all the cards that have "planeswalkers you control have X". Because this is like Amass in that you can't have multiple Jace tokens via Empower Jace, it's not too abusive. Obviously if you just want to pump up a Jace you've made a token of to ultimate very quickly it's a way to do that, but it'll take a lot of mana. If this mechanic returns with other planeswalkers, which I could easily see with Empower Chandra and Empower Liliana in other sets, it could be a pretty interesting set of abilities.

FromTheShire: This is a pretty neat and mechanically interesting ability. At this point I'm wildly disconnected from the story and its justification for these tokens so I'm not sure exactly how likely we actually are to see this pop up again on other walkers, but the space is certainly wide open. There's a lot of nifty little tricks you can pull now, and I'm sure more will be discovered as people start playing with the cards. In 60 card there are a couple of quite powerful seeming options like Jace's Machinations that give you a massive amount of loyalty for cheap, and I believe this is the first time we are going to have planeswalkers be legal in Pauper so it will be cool to see what people brew there. Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Heartwood Tokens

Red & Green have a new token to build around in Reality Fracture: Heartwood. This is like a less conditional Powerstone token, with it usually coming in untapped, and having the capacity to add {R} or {G}. Often, it’s tied to the signature spell of the Konstrari mages in the RG color identity, being a 3 mana Prepared Sorcery called Soul Tether, although there are several other ways to produce them in Gruul.

Saffgor: In terms of mana rock tokens that stick around, Heartwood is probably the strongest we’ve seen. Less conditional than Vibranium or Powerstones, more enduring than Treasure or Gold, and fairly accessible for RGx Commanders. We’ve already seen a half-dozen genuinely playable cards which create these, so I’d expect to see Heartwood at the Commander table with reasonable frequency.

BPhillipYork: Red/Green having a mana rock artifact token feels very off to me, like color-pie wise, which is part of the point of the set. These tokens though are potentially very broken. They enter untapped, there's ways to duplicate them again, or use effects like Doubling Season. In the end these will probably end up like Powerstone tokens, not all that impactful except for decks that really focus on them.

FromTheShire: The fact that these enter untapped, in the token doubling color, means that while they are going to be quite useful little mana rocks as a baseline sometimes they are going to juice a turn through the roof. The main question will be if you can make and utilize them well enough to justify them being more fragile than regular old land based ramp since you're in green already. We have been getting a slow trickle of RG artifacts matter commanders like Roxanne, Starfall Savant and Bello, Bard of the Brambles that enjoy these as well, especially Roxanne.

Returning Mechanics

Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Prepare

Prepare is back, and its inclusion here really makes Secrets of Strixhaven and Reality Fracture feel akin to a 2-set block. Creatures with a Prepared Spell are either Unprepared, or Prepared, and in the latter case a copy of their Prepared Spell sits in exile, waiting to be put into the stack & cast during its appropriate timing window. Once a Prepared Spell enters the stack, its linked object, the Creature, becomes Unprepared. Unlike Strixhaven, the majority of Prepare Creatures in this set share one of five Spells, representing the regimented doctrine of Hexhaven, so if you see a multicolored Prepare Spell, expect it on more than one card in the set.

Saffgor: I think, now having seen all of Reality Fracture, Prepare might be the most successful ‘double spell’ mechanic we’ve had since Adventures. That’s a high bar, but I do genuinely love the mechanic, and repeatable casts make Spells you’d otherwise not include in an eternal-format deck far more worthwhile. I think the actual scaffolding of Prepare is a bit weird (keeping a copy of a Spell in exile until you need it is weird, and didn’t “work” until the SOS FAQ), but once you have a general understanding it’s easy to love. One thing worth noting is that there’s cards in the set aimed at quietly ‘teaching’ some of its intricacies, with Heartwood Crafter supplying mana for Spells cast from outside your hand, and its Soul Tether being in exile, e.g. outside of your hand. Cards which teach their own mechanics scratch the design itch that a lot of modern Magic tends not to.

BPhillipYork: I like prepare, though it's basically an ETB with additional costs, or sort of a weird version of monstrous, a one shot ability unless you have ways to flicker it (though monstrous is the same). I think it's a useful design tool, and I'd like to see more things that care about using prepared spells show up. It's also neat to see iconic spells like Swords to Plowshares or Lightning Bolt though hopefully they don't just exploit them for nostalgia.

FromTheShire: Prepared spells have proven to be quite successful so far, with a number of them being playable and no hideously broken misses yet. As long as we don't wind up with a busted way to mass prepare at some point I think we should be okay. Credit: Wizards of the Coast.

Cameo Mechanics

As you can tell, the number of core mechanics in Reality Fracture is fairly minimal, which is a shock given the overall complexity of most modern sets. That's because part of the design of the set is predicated not on introducing new keywords or abilities, but calling back to previous planes and characters via 'Cameo Mechanics', a concept introduced in 2023. Split Second, Exhaust, Convoke, and more all return here, giving many of the Echoverse cards the energy of being from a set like Commander Masters—a celebration of Magic's history.

Saffgor: As the number of sets each year has climbed, I think this is a smart move on the part of the designers; gone are the days of five flashy new mechanics in something like a Ravnica set, because with ~6 sets each year that represents an information overload to all but the most enfranchised. Every set is someone's first set, so while there might be a bit of confusion over these one-off mechanics, with Commander being the most popular format basically all players will come to see them anyways. The average complexity is up, and it seems reasonable to expect the average willingness to digest complexity of a new player likely is as well.

BPhillipYork: There's a bunch of weird static abilities showing up, this one in particular is really kind of nuts. It's fun to have callbacks to specific mechanics and I wish they'd do more of this, so you could build a Commander deck around Arcane cards or something like that, though "everything has split second" isn't so much about split second cards.

FromTheShire: I would 100% be in favor of more sets like this. Magic already has so, so many mechanics (many of them functioning extremely similarly) that sometimes it really begs the question why we needed a different keyword for it in the newest set, only for it to be immediately abandoned. Maybe it all boils down to Kicker being such a good, foundational mechanic they can't get away from repackaging it as something new over and over again.

Next Time: The Set’s Multicolor & Colorless Cards

That wraps up our look at the mechanics of Reality Fracture. We’ll be back later to look at the most noteworthy cards in the set, starting with the Multicolor and Colorless cards, and then Monocolor options in the following articles.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@goonhammer.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don’t forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and more.

title: D&D's Paladin is unrecognizable with this new World of Warcraft subclass
content:
The first episodes of the new D&D Dungeon Masters series actual play show have aired, and fans are getting their first glimpse of the many new features coming in the upcoming World of Warcraft crossover book. That includes the undead Death Knight - ably played in the series by goth fave Neil Newbon - a new 'hero class' that turns the Paladin on its head.

Influencers with early access to the book have been providing the information in a condensed format, and this article is indebted to the YouTuber Insight Check - you can find his coverage in the video below if you prefer listening to reading.

Surprisingly, it looks like the new WoW supplement is going to take the most innovative approach to DnD classes of any 5.5 book to date.

To play a Death Knight, you'll field a Paladin with the new Oath of the Ebon Blade subclass. Unusually, this subclass rewrites level one and level two class features from the base Paladin. If you have DM permission - and agree to be bound by your choice of subclass from level one - you can actually create a level one Death Knight.

It's one of three 'hero classes' in the new book, along with the Demon Hunter and Evoker. In WoW selecting one of these classes will see you start the game at a higher level. The Demon Hunter is a Ranger subclass which also alters its base class, while the Evoker is a little less intrusive, modifying the Sorcerer's Draconic Sorcery subclass.

Death Knight Class Features

Death Knights are Undead, and no matter what your creature type was to start with, once you pledge to the Ebon Blade, you swap it out. This means losing the Humanoid subtype, making you immune to Hold Person - yay! - but also immune to Cure Wounds and Raise Dead - boo.

All Death Knights get the Runeforging feature, letting them inscribe magical runes onto their weapon, picking from three specializations - Blood, Frost, or Unholy. These don't have any direct mechanical effect, but they're basically cosmetic - other subclass features might key off them.

Death Knights replace the Paladin's Level 1 ability Lay On Hands with Death Coil. Instead of a pool of dice for healing, you get a pool of negative energy d8s for draining life - a number equals to one plus your Charisma modifier, which refreshes each long rest. Using these dice is a bonus action, which allows you to spend up to your Charisma modifier in dice, roll them, and force a target you can see within 60 feet to make a Constitution save. They'll take the full dice roll if they fail, or half damage on a success. You can choose to heal undead targets, which includes yourself.

At level 2, Runic Smite replaces the regular Paladin's Smite. It's basically a reskin, replacing the spell Divine Smite with Rune Strike, which functions exactly the same, except that it deals Necrotic damage rather than Radiant damage, and deals bonus damage to Celestial targets instead of the Undead. According to Insight Check, the majority of spells in the book aren't just reskins - but a few are.

Forsaken Species

The other part of Newbon's new character, Glaive, is the new Forsaken DnD species. It's not a mandatory requirement for becoming a Deathknight, but it does synergise well. The Forsaken are Undead with souls loosely tethered to their bodies, and accordingly their Creature Type is Undead. This doesn't just affect spell targeting - they have a suite of immunities and resistances to go along with it.

Specifically, they're resistant to Necrotic damage, have advantage on saving throws to avoid or end the Charmed or Frightened conditions, and can't gain Exhaustion levels from dehydration, malnutrition, or suffocation. They don't need to sleep, can't be magically put to sleep, and can finish a Long Rest in four hours of conscious inactivity - presumably this is indistinguishable from rigor mortis, and is quite alarming for any elves attempting to meditate.

The Forsaken get Darkvision up to 60 feet - who doesn't? - and then a handy little combat trick called Touch of the Grave. This is a once per long rest ability that can be used when dealing damage to a creature. This lets the Forsaken roll a number of d4 equal to their Proficiency Bonus, dealing that much extra Necrotic damage. However much damage the target actually suffers (after resistance), the Forsaken gets to heal.

The additional healing and minor melee damage burst seems like a great synergy for the Death Knight. My thoughts are immediately drawn to a Forsaken Rogue whose cons take advantage of not needing to eat or breathe. What do you think of these new undead character building options? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Total War Warhammer Lords of the End Times
content:
The phrase “End Times” is a loaded one to many of the folks who frequent this website. It refers to the sequence of events that led to the shuttering of the world of Warhammer Fantasy which recently returned as Warhammer Old World. Fantasy contained a lot of beloved characters, many done dirty by the wrap up of their stories all happening quickly and in sequence. Because of that, and the killing of an entire game system, the End Times left a bad taste in a lot of long time player’s mouths. After 10 years, the Total War: Warhammer series is doing their own End Times with a new DLC release, and no doubt are looking to have a better landing than their tabletop predecessors.

Thank you to SEGA for providing us with access to the Lord of the End Times DLC. 

What You’re Getting

The Lords of the End Times is a pack of 4 DLCs, each containing a legendary lord for Total War Warhammer 3. Each of these DLCs can be played stand alone, meaning you can play the Nagash campaign without owning Total War Warhammer 3 or any other DLC which is pretty exciting. Each Lord is part of a preexisting faction (or a collection of them) and provides their own twist on their established formulas. Available is Boris Todbringer (Empire), Glottkin (Warriors of Chaos), Thanquol (Skaven), and Nagash (Kinda Tomb Kings I guess maybe but really all the undead factions at once; it's kinda nuts).

The Lords

Boris offers some more melee focused troops to the Empire roster. Sworn to the god Ulfric, his guys are largely wolf themed and focused around either anchoring the line or hitting your opponent hard. There’s not a ton to write home about here, as mostly everything has a comparative unit that’s already in the roster (shield infantry but elite, knights but more durable) but what’s here fills out the Empire roster to let you build any sort of army you can imagine. You can have your gunline, scrappy blitz infantry, or a tech-y magic focused force. The new units are a nice mix of low, mid and high tier so you’ll see a lot of new stuff across all steps of your campaign.

Mechanically, Boris focuses around his Temple of Ulfric, which can give you some faction-wide effects that can bolster your forces and the Defense of the Drakenwald system that has you fighting on going beastmen attacks as the campaign goes on. The latter is the narrative focus of the campaign, as Boris preps for the ongoing chaos incursions he’ll be looking to settle his grudge he has with Kazarak One-Eye in a climatic cinematic battle. All the lords have a quest like this and little narrative blurbs breadcrumbed along the way which helps guide the player towards different goals.

Next up, The Glottkin are somewhat your standard warriors of Chaos flair. You get access to some new fast moving cheap infantry in the form of Flayerkin, a new giant, and a slew of Blightking variants. This is one thing a lot of folks may have complaints about in this DLC; there are a lot of reskins. That said, the design around these reskins is definitely not slapdash. For example, in addition to the above units, the Glottkin get access to four legendary heroes, three of which -- the Maggoth Lords -- are reskins of each other, but each has a distinct skill tree and battlefield role and one can be used as a legendary lord when you unlock them. While they may look similar you’ll be using them very differently and can theme entire armies around each one of them.

Mechanically the Glottkin have the standard Warriors of Chaos systems of vassalizing Norsca fractions by roughing them up and using those vassals to fund your war into forces of Order. Special to them though are the Gifts of Nurgle, which are buffs you can give to Lords and Heroes that can do things like spread plagues or change the actions they can do on the campaign map, and the Gardens of Corruption, which basically give you a settlement from the Nurgle daemon faction, giving you access to their roster and plagues. With the Warriors of Chaos recruitment system and the summoned daemons you get from the Gardens you can pop up a formidable force in a turn assuming you can financially support it, allowing you to make lightning assaults wherever you need them. 

I spent the most time with the Glottkin in my time prepping for the review, upgrading marauders all the way to Blightkings and achieving their short victory by conquering Altdorf. The narrative beats and the way the game guides you along an “ideal” path is a welcome change of pace from other Immortal Empires campaigns, giving you enough short term goals to keep you engaged beyond just attacking the next settlement. In battles, the Glottkin are an absolute terror as well. Once you get some regeneration on the trio they’re almost impossible to take down.

Where the Glottkin may be familiar, Nagash is altogether different. Nagash uses the full rosters from all the undead factions in the game. You want an army of grave guard backed up by Vampire Coast artillery? You can do that. You want a monster mash of all the undead big guys? Absolutely. Getting all the best heroes together for a single entity doomstack? You got it. In addition, you can confederate most of the big factions as well as some fresher faces via the Mortarch system, allowing you to pay some money after a set of conditions are met to automatically grab all their assets.

You also get the most insane tech system ever introduced in this series via the Black Pyramid. If you’ve played Path of Exile or Final Fantasy X, this will be familiar. It's a sphere grid. The thing that's messed up is that every single node on this thing is useful and a lot are transformative to how your units function. This is probably the most impressive thing in the set of DLCs; if you’re looking to get just one lord, pick Nagash for this reason alone.

On the battlefield, Nagash is also a monster in his own right. With access to the new lore of Undeath and the massive buffs you can get to his spell casting he can out-heal and out damage most things in front of him. He’s no slouch in combat either, as long as you keep him healed up (which is trivial with his abilities) he can solo entire low tier settlement garrisons. His new units add some nice spice to existing undead rosters, with spirit hosts giving you a new type of chaff that are a fantastic tarpit if your opponent doesn’t have magical attacks, Morghast providing fast moving monstrous infantry that can hang for a while unsupported and the Khemric Titan which is a big bug made of rocks that shoot lasers.

Last-last but not least-least is everyone's favorite grey seer; Thanquol. Mechanically, Thanquol isn’t too different from other Skaven lords, but gets an additional mechanic called Master Plans. These plans can be a bit confusing on their face but in practice are pretty straight forward. Basically you assign one of your four underlings to do a plan; this can be something like massing a garbage army to attack a settlement, stealing warpstone (Thanquol’s special currency) and money from another faction, or doing some more specialist stuff like summoning one of the new Verminlords. Once you start your plan, every turn your underling will draw some “schemes” from a deck that will determine what you’re getting out of your plan, the longer you let the plan cook though, “complications” will arise that can do things like kill your massing units or remove money from your pot. The nice thing is these plans are relatively cheap to enact so you can keep spamming them.

On the battlefield Thanquol is mostly unimpressive until he gets his mount Boneripper, at which point he becomes a ranged (or melee if you’re inclined) powerhouse. If you’ve ever used warpflamers and said “wow these are pretty good” but bemoaned their speed and inability to hang in melee, Thanquol does it all. The same can be said for his additions to the roster. The headliners are the Stormfiend variants that come in 6 flavors: fire, machine gun, poison wind launchers, grinder fist, big spiky balls, electro fists. These are all reskins of each other, but the utility added to the Skaven roster for a durable weapons platform or brawler unit that can be in sustained combat can’t be denied. In addition, there’s stuff like the low tier Pusbags or the high tier Warp-Doom Magma Cannon that adds a nice bit of variety between high and low tier units. In addition, Skaven can now recruit Verminlords, the greater daemons of the faction, to lead armies. These give some pretty amazing buffs and are strong combatants in their own right.

Closing Time

All of the above isn’t a comprehensive list of what’s in this DLC, but even then there’s plenty of meat on this bone. And that doesn’t even take into account the 9.0 update that’s releasing alongside it with a ton of quality of life improvements and Neferatta. Overall though what I imagine folks will want to know is “Is this worth it?” If you’re a veteran of the series looking for something new, this is absolutely a great get. Each lord brings exactly what you’re looking for and a ton of cool mechanics to sink your teeth into. If you’re looking to hop into the Total War Warhammer ecosystem with this DLC though… I’ll be honest these are some of the most complex characters and factions that are in the game. All of them have mechanics you’ll have to respect or you can easily bork your save, and even when I knew what I was looking at, things like the Black Pyramid and the Master Plans had me scratching my head a bit. If you’re up to the challenge and love reading A Lot when diving into a strategy game, there’s a lot to chew on here, but ironically the End Times are gonna demand a lot of your time. 

All that said there’s so much love here that if you’re just coming in as a person who loves Warhammer you’ll find a lot to like. When Gotrek and Felix showed up and ruined my Master Plan with Thanquol where I was trying to steal from Nuln, it felt incredibly apt. Nagash snowballing into an unbeatable force and casting a billion spells truly felt like he does on the tabletop. The characters all ooze with personality, and clearly feel like they belong in the world they inhabit. Even with 20ish hours under my belt in this DLC alone, I can tell you my time here isn’t quite at its end.

title: How to Paint Everything: Marvel Crisis Protocol - Omega Sentinel
content:
Hey everybody, I'm back again with How to Paint Everything: Marvel Crisis Protocol, and today we are taking a look at Omega Sentinel from the new Sentinels affiliated Character Pack, featuring Bastion, Nimrod, and Omega Sentinel.

Omega Sentinel boasts a few different configurations for you to customize her look. Since I was first introduced to her in the House of X/Powers of X comic series, I decided to go with the Mega Buster style gun arm, back spikes and her bald head. But you have the choice for a masked head with hair and a few other arm options too.

Like Nimrod, Omega Sentinel's armor is mostly white, but this time we also have some red and black accents too. Her bald head has the markings on it, so you can paint it either with them or without them. I decided to keep it looking like her character card art and added them to it. We'll also go over some quick and dirty non-metallic metal as well as the customary Sentinel energy glow effects.

Below you'll find the handy paint chart, as usual. Featuring all of the colors that were used to paint her up. So, let's get rolling on it!

credit - Brushwizard

Head Skin Tone

Basecoat - Army Painter Dragon Red

Shadows - Army Painter Magecast Magenta

Layer - Army Painter Dragon Red, Army Painter Angelic Red

Highlight - Previous Mix, Reaper Rosy Skin

Highlight - Previous Mix, More Reaper Rosy Skin

Omega Sentinel's head started with a basecoat of Dragon Red. The recesses of her eye sockets, under her chin and any other shaded areas were then painted Magecast Magenta. Highlights started with a layer of Dragon Red mixed with Angelic Red. I then added Rosy Skin to the mix to brighten it up a bit, followed by another highlight layer with a bit more Rosy Skin added to the mix.

White Head Markings

Basecoat - AK Interactive Black

Layer - AK Interactive White

Shadow - AK Interactive Pastel Blue

The white markings on her head started with a base of Black to define the shapes. Then I painted White inside the shapes, leaving a black line around the perimeter. Shaded areas were given a layer of Pastel Blue to darken them up a bit and added color variation.

White Armor

Basecoat - Citadel Grey Seer Spray Primer

Layer - AK Interactive Pastel Blue

Layer - AK Interactive Ivory

Dark Lining - AK Interactive French Blue

Highlight - AK Interactive White

As with most of my recent white armors, I start with a basecoat of Grey Seer primer. The non-metallic metal effect started with a layer of Pastel Blue, making sure to leave some of the Grey Seer visible on the surface. Next, the reflective surface highlights continue with a layer of Ivory on top of the Pastel Blue layer, leaving some of the previous layer showing as well. The armor panel lines were dark lined with French Blue, and then all of the armor panels were edge highlighted with White.

Red Armor Sections

Basecoat - Army Painter Dragon Red

Shadows - Army Painter Dragon Red, Army Painter Angel Green

Layer - Army Painter Angelic Red

Highlight - Army Painter Flickering Flame

Highlight - AK Interactive White

Like her head, the red sections of her armor started with Dragon Red. This time, shadows were painted by mixing Angel Green into Dragon Red to create a darker red; this was painted into any areas that would be darker or in shadow. Highlights started by painting a layer of Angelic Red over the Dragon Red areas, leaving some Dragon Red visible. It was then highlighted and edge highlighted with Flickering Flame and White.

Black Striping

Basecoat - AK Interactive Black

Layer - AK Interactive Black: AK Interactive French Blue

Highlight - AK Interactive French Blue

The black striping of her suit started with a basecoat of Black. It was then highlighted with a mix of Black and French Blue, followed by a simple final highlight of French Blue on its own.

Metals

Basecoat - AK Interactive French Blue

Shadows - Thinned AK Interactive Dark Sea Blue

Highlight - AK Interactive French Blue

Highlight - AK Interactive White

Dark Lining - AK Interactive Black

All of the metal areas of this model were painted with a base coat of French Blue. Next, I thinned Dark Sea Blue and painted all of the metal with it to get that color into any recesses in the bionics. It was then highlighted using French Blue and then White. Shadows were reinforced by painting Black into any recesses that I felt needed a bit more oomph.

Glowing Armor Lights

Basecoat - AK Interactive White

Layer - Lethal Shadows Fluorescent Red

All of her light effects were painted White, followed by Fluorescent Red.

Gun Arm Glow

Basecoat - AK Interactive White

Layer - Lethal Shadows Fluorescent Light Orange

Layer - Lethal Shadows Fluorescent Red

The glow inside the barrel of her gun was given a basecoat of White. I then used Fluorescent Light Orange inside the entire area and then Fluorescent Red around the perimeter.

Hoses

Basecoat - AK Interactive Black

Highlight - AK Interactive Dark Sea Blue

Highlight - AK Interactive Dark Sea Blue: AK Interactive Ivory

The hoses that are holding her up off of her base started with a basecoat of Black. It was given a layer of Dark Sea Blue to make them look a bit rubbery, and then highlighted with a mix of Dark Sea Blue and Ivory.

Concrete Basing

Basecoat - Citadel Stormvermin Fur

Stipple - Army Painter Ash Grey

Stipple - Army Painter Brigade Grey

Wash - Citadel Nuln Oil

As usual, the concrete basing started with a base layer of Stormvermin Fur, followed by stippling of Ash Grey and Brigade Grey. All of the concrete sections were then washed with Nuln Oil to tie it together and add some shadows to the recesses in the base.

Dirt Basing

Basecoat - Citadel Gorthor Brown

Wash - Citadel Agrax Earthshade

Any dirt on the base was painted Gorthor Brown and then washed with Agrax Earthshade.

credit - Brushwizard

With that, Omega Sentinel is now ready to blast her way onto the tabletop! You can find Omega Sentinel alongside Bastion and Nimrod, the Hunter in the MCP09 Bastion, Nimrod & Omega Sentinel Character Pack, which is now available for purchase at your FLGS or online. As always, a big thank you goes out to Atomic Mass Games and Asmodee for sending this character pack my way. It's very much appreciated!

Have you picked up this character pack and painted up the models? Join us in the Marvel: Crisis Protocol channel of the Tabletop Battles Discord server! Or you can find me on Instagram or Bluesky as well. I am always interested in seeing what the community has going on with MCP.

title: Wingspan board game designer Elizabeth Hargrave wants to take you bird-watching in Colombia
content:
Wake up gang, new luxury board game holiday just dropped. Avian tourism team Good Bird is offering a 10-day trip to Colombia to view the country's most beautiful birds. You'll be joined by tabletop designer Elizabeth Hargrave, best known for her smash-hit bird board game, Wingspan.

The trip, set for January 11 - 20 2027, is apparently a celebration of the Wingspan Americas expansion that released later this year. We gave it a 9/10 review, so hopefully this trip lives up to the same hype - especially as it costs around $4,000 to attend. International flights, some meals, and health insurance are not included.

It's a pricey trip, but it promises a spectacular show of feathers. Day one covers arrival and orientation, but day two sends you on a bird walk up a mountain to see tanagers, toucanets, barbets, and more. There's time for tea tasting, and you might get a game of Wingspan or two in the evening.

Day three offers a birding-tour combo at a coffee farm, with afternoons reserved for rest (and more Wingspan). That's a trend for most of the days' itineraries.

Day four takes you to Laguna Sonso and Río Cauca to see aquatic birds and raptors, while day five sees you birding with local youth clubs in an urban setting. Day six features a hummingbird garden, barbet feedings, and a hunt for a chestnut wood quail.

Day seven promises "Andes-Pacific transition zone birding, including visit to Andean cock-of-the-rock lek and another hummingbird garden". The next day, you'll bird along San Cipriano River. Lastly, day nine features more urban birding near your lodge, before you depart on day 10.

Only 12 spaces are available for the trip. If you want to be one of them, you can find the details on Good Bird's website. Or, if you want to read more about the best board games of all time, hit up our dedicated guide - or ask for our top picks in the Wargamer Discord.

title: New Blood Bowl videogame is "a unique chance" to redo the game after BB3's mess of a launch, says developer
content:
The launch of Blood Bowl 3 in spring of 2023 was something that a lot of Blood Bowl fans would rather forget: disgruntled community organizers faced game breaking bugs, inadequate admin tools, and communities split between the new game and the still-live Blood Bowl 2. I'm not about to forget it, since I'm terminally embarrassed by the naïvely positive review I gave to the game - and neither is Mathieu Valero, a programmer at Cyanide Studio who worked on the game. "It was a mess, like there's no two ways about it", he says, when I meet up  to interview him about the next entry in the series, 'Warhammer: Blood Bowl'.

Valero is a programmer, and he's here for the interview because the team member Cyanide Studio originally planned to send was called away for a family emergency. Programmers are usually locked up far away from journalists, toiling in the code mines while game designers or executive producers talk to the press using small words we can understand. I find Valero refreshingly frank about the coal face of game development.

"Blood Bowl Three and Blood Bowl Two should not have coexisted", he admits. In 2020, Games Workshop released a major update to tabletop Blood Bowl in the form of 'Second Season Edition', which meant that Blood Bowl 2 was now running on an outdated version of the rules. "In a vacuum, if we had been apt to do it, it just would have been an update [to Blood Bowl 2]" Valero says, "but at the time, we were not doing live ops, we had no idea. The tech couldn't follow, Blood Bowl 2 was way too old, and we needed to update everything". If they wanted to keep developing Blood Bowl, it had to be in a new game.

Valero remembers the launch of Blood Bowl 3 as "dark times" when some people left the company. He says he stuck it out "because I'm stubborn". That was the low point for Cyanide - but the studio stayed afloat, Blood Bowl 3 stayed online, and Mathieu stayed with the team. And as the old saying goes, when you're at rock bottom, the only way is up.

The right stuff

"From that point on we learned so much", Valero says. He's not certain exactly when things began to turn around, but he thinks that September 2024's Season Six - which added halflings and goblins - was a likely point. It was still "a little bit bumpy, still super demanding on the team", but "from the outside, [the game] starts to look like something".

He doesn't say it explicitly, but I put together from context that this is the point he thinks Cyanide began to successfully deliver 'live ops development' - a way of handling a game's code that makes it possible to continually inject new content to the live game. It's the foundation for most contemporary online multiplayer games.

"From season six [onwards] we've had six more seasons of live ops, [learning] what it takes to make such a game", he says. "That's been a learning process, a demanding one".

The upcoming Warhammer: Blood Bowl is more like a definitive edition than a new game, given to all BB3 owners as a free upgrade, running on the same videogame engine but implementing the updated 'third season edition' of tabletop Blood Bowl rules that Games Workshop released in 2025. Valero calls it "a unique chance to redo [the game] with all we've learned… starting from almost two years of live experience". He repeats himself emphatically: "this is a unique chance, it doesn't happen".

Fundamentals

In the first article I wrote up about the new edition of Blood Bowl, I focused on just the new and updated features Valero described for the game. In our interview, he's remarkably candid about all the areas where Blood Bowl 3 has been lacking, before describing how Warhammer: Blood Bowl will improve on them. Here's how he describes improvements in player onboarding between the two games: in BB3 "we had none - now we have some… It's hard to advertise because it's so obvious, this was such a blatant blind spot".

"The UI has been significantly revamped", he adds, "first and foremost the homepage, which was a gigantic waste of space, now it's going to be a customizable set of tiles". These will include shortcuts to the current seasonal competitions, and "when you go on the main page of a competition you can pin it to your home if you wanna go back to it". The tiles are being driven by two years of user data about what players actually interact with.

User data also gives the figure that players play 70 to 80 percent of their games solo, against the AI: AI which was, at Blood Bowl 3's launch, so lacking that Valero dismisses it entirely. "We didn't have an AI - now we do", and it's apparently capable of beating new players and giving experienced players a decent match. "There are still a bunch of factions and builds that it's more able to play well: you want to give it Guard and Block, and don't go fancy with the combos that a human would be able to do", but "give something reliable to the AI, and you're gonna have a game to play".

New ways to play

If this gives the impression that Valero is cautious or downbeat, that's hardly the case - his excitement for the game comes off him in waves. It helps that he's a massive tabletop Blood Bowl nerd, preferring fast and squishy teams.

Later, when we're at a meal hosted by publisher Slitherine's marketing team, he enthusiastically analyses the changes that Games Workshop made for Blood Bowl Third Season edition: he had expected the new 'Secure the Ball' action to be a free boost to bash teams, but finds there are often interesting decisions to make when securing would cost a few extra spaces of movement compared to attempting a pick up.

He's particularly nerdy about fast playing versions of Blood Bowl. "We've been looking into how Games Workshop makes Blood Bowl palatable [for new players], simpler, more streamlined version: Blood Bowl Sevens is one, Blitz Bowl is one". He says "I'm a super fan of the scoring system of Blitz Bowl - you don't score touchdowns, you score points for SPPs". "We have this mode [in our test builds]", he whispers conspiratorially. "It's not going to be released for the demo, I don't know if it's going to make it [in the release version], but maybe it's going to happen later down the line".

And then there's Blood Bowl Rumble, a seven-a-side mode that is similar to Blood Bowl Sevens. "It's an attempt inspired by different sources to make a more streamlined version of the game, and it borrows a lot from Sevens, but it's not exactly that", Valero says. "This is a thing we overlooked for years - we are a digital version of Blood Bowl, and what's easy for us is different from what's easy for Games Workshop". So while Cyanide has been "hardcore" about implementing the original Blood Bowl rulebook for Elevens, when comparing Sevens to Rumble "the name is different because we want to keep some leeway about what the streamlining actually entails".

He outlines a vision to me, though emphasises that this is his preference for the mode, and may not be the one that ships. "Sevens is known to not stand a lot of skills; it's really nice with fresh teams, if you want to balance a bit some factions need to start with a little bit more, but you can't have seven players with seven skills". So what about a version of the game without progression - indeed, without team building, like Blitz Bowl? Heresy to the traditionalists, but if the goal is to onboard players to Blood Bowl, this could be a way to introduce them to playing the game and mastering different teams before they worry about team construction and progression choices.

My impression of Valero's openness is that he's genuinely confident. He's happy to talk about Cyanide Studio at its lowest ebb and acknowledge all its inadequacies because - as he sees it - the future looks good.

If you're a Blood Bowl player, digital or physical, hop into the Wargamer Discord community!

title: [AoS] Tabletop Battles Reviews: Age of Sigmar Fall 2026 Battlescroll
content:
Just a week before LVO, GW drops a surprise Battlescroll, just in time for list submissions. The state of the meta has improved a lot since Aqshy began, with a lot of armies falling within that desired 45-55% range. There are some pretty extreme outliers though, such Cities of Sigmar and Fyreslayers on the higher end and Ossiarch Bonereapers, Skaven and Stormcast on the lower end. So will these changes be enough to impact the tournament right before one of the biggest events of the year? We're going to go through what's hot and what's not below.

If you want to follow along, you can find the Battlescroll on the Games Workshop Downloads page.

Core Rule Changes

Not many here. Due to the absolute deluge of generic foot heroes the game is full of right now, and because list building as it stands can make using them difficult, a lot of heroes had a rider added that allows them to be a "sub-commander" for a lot of bigger heroes. There's too many to list here, but basically every generic foot and cavalry hero got this treatment, which is going to help condense a lot of listbuilding. Most importantly, it means that bringing a Wizard or Priest may not cost you an entire new regiment now.

Similarly, many Warcry warbands had their "cannot be reinforced" rule pulled. This isn't quite universal, but it's close. Again, we'll note any interesting ones in the individual army entries.

Order

Cities of Sigmar

Kicking off with some pretty big changes here. War Hydras have gained a lot of traction in the past few weeks, when people noticed that killing them is a gigantic pain in the ass. Previously, you got to roll a fistful of dice whenever it died and if you got any 5s, it didn't die. Very cheap for that, and could keep the enemy clogged up for quite some time for something not even that many points. In exchange now, it just has Heal (6) at end of turn, which probably means it's dead now. Being a legends model, GW probably prefers it that way.

On the points front, as expected Cavaliers took a massive hit. +30 for 5. The unit was far too cheap for what it did and given most people ran 2 reinforced units of 10, that's 120 points and probably will need to be sussed out what else can be done with the army. Along those lines, the Cavalier Marshal went up 10 and Steelhelms up 20, which is a lot for a unit designed to take hits and then die. Taken together these are huge blows to the current Cities of Sigmar meta lists and will likely radically change the makeup of lists going forward.

There are some point drops, as a consolation prize. One of the Cogforts, Zenestra, and Gallants getting some point drops, to name a few.

Verdict: Loser

Daughters of Khaine

Daughters are currently in the "Acceptable" winrate, but they are really only barely at 55%, so time for points hikes on the expected stuff. Morathi, Blood Sisters and Scourge of Aqshy Melusai Ironscale went up and that's going to hurt big time. You're looking at another 60-80 points on your average list (assuming 1 or 2 reinforced Blood Sisters) which is probably going to force cutting down on the chaff even further. Removing Morathi entirely may enter the discussion as her cost gets extremely high, but give how much Aqshy rules love her tail attack (3 Damage 6 attacks!) it's a hard argument to make.

Verdict: Loser

Fyreslayers

Fyreslayers have been suffering through most of fourth edition; as one of the last armies to get a Battletome they have had to struggle through a pretty barren list of warscroll options, only to get the shot in the arm they needed with Ghyran giving them a better Son on Magmadroth. Then punished for their hubris, the points have dropped down on basically everything ever since, to a point that combined with the Scourge of Aqshy buffs, the army has gotten a bit out of control.

A bit of tech that's become popular is the new Blazing Impetus prayer in Scourge of Aqshy. A free movement in the Hero phase, it's mostly fine except for when a unit drops in from deep strike thanks to the Runesmiter, and then gets to move 4", making a 5" charge a lot more reliable.

The point changes were pretty fair all things considered. Bump to Hearthguard Berserkers, Flameseekers (both kinds) and the Runesmiter. Foot Heroes can now join up with Runefathers and Sons as sub-commanders.

The Elephant in the room is, of course, the army is on borrowed time so they likely weren't interested in making too many changes, just enough to get through until the new Khazalite book is out and legal.

Verdict: Loser

Idoneth Deepkin

Real boring. Just some price drops on heroes nobody was using, and likely will continue to not use. There was a rules change to the Scourge of Aqshy trait Abyssal Dweller which used to subtract the battle round from the movement characteristic, likely changed because it was absolutely overbearing to slower armies like Nurgle and Helsmiths.

The army is in an OK spot, could be better but could be a lot worse too.

Verdict: Loser

Kharadron Overlords

No rules changes, 20 point drop on both kinds of big boat is nice, and Endrinriggers getting a slight drop is cute, might see more of them around as a result. Otherwise nothing too exciting here. The army is in the 45% win rate category but it's barely hanging on and might need help later.

Verdict: Winner

Lumineth Realm-lords

After a really strong start in 4th, and a pretty solid book, Lumineth have struggled a bit as the points kept going up. So now they're letting off the gas a bit, mostly focusing on bringing the points on Alarith stone units down, with cuts to Stoneguard, Stone Mage and Spirit of the Mountain. 

Ellania and Ellathor going up another 20 points is probably not unexpected, but  does hurt the most common list building. Thankfully, not much else in those lists is heavily impacted.

Yrdrilan Riverblades losing their "cannot be reinforced" rule is probably one of the bigger beneficiaries of it. It was a popular unit and being able to make them stronger is probably a good thing for trying to assassinate tougher heroes.

Verdict: Neutral

Seraphon

Seraphon have been eating pretty good since their Asterisms were updated, and also have a book coming soon, so it's likely they didn't want to make too many changes. Being able to put Skinks as sub-commanders under Slaan is nice, and a few point drops on Oldbloods both on foot and mounted might help their use a bit. It's fine, if boring.

Verdict: Slight Winner

Stormcast Eternals

I hate having to make judgement calls for Stormcast. Every quarterly update they fiddle with the numbers and drop the points on some unit I've never heard of and next week it's the new meta.

In this case it's nothing but point drops. Knight-Draconis and Stormdrake Guard going down is nice for people who miss running dragons, as they haven't seen play in a bit. This probably gets them a bit closer. Tornus the Redeemed sees limited play so hopefully a point drop will help him see more play. Gryphounds down to 80 makes them good chaff pieces, probably good play there. Knight Arcanum might be able to slip into more lists now that it can be a subcommander is cheaper.

The only thing that stings is Questor did not get the "cannot reinforce is gone now" bonus most Warcry warbands got, which probably dashed a lot of hopes at hearing that. Sucks for them, but that probably was going too far.

Verdict: Winner

Sylvaneth

Points hikes on some of the staples. Warsong Revenant went up 20 points but you probably still take him; as the army's lone priest you kinda gotta. Twistweald isn't required but was quite popular for its control ability and it did also go up 20 points. You can reinforce it, but you likely won't wanna do that anyway.

Being able to put the Branchwych in as a subcommander is a small bit of comfort,  since often people would have to make a detachment solely dedicated to it, so being able to go from 4 to 3 drops might make a difference in deployment.

Verdict: Loser

Chaos

Blades of Khorne

Pretty mild overall. After suffering from the Bloodbound Army of Renown being too damn good, and then nerfed, GW seems to have considered it safe to bring Deathbringer  and Skullgrinder out of probation, just a bit with a -10 to each. Otherwise just a small drop to the cannon and the Scourge of Aqshy Bloodletters.

Verdict: Winner

Disciples of Tzeentch

Some technical changes, Smoke and Mirrors had a minor change to wording to clarify "Set up" means "set up on the battlefield" to make it in accordance with usual legal ruling. The actual important change here is that Fate Points are now capped at 9. Aside from being a fluffy option, it prevents abuse around the lore spell Infernal Gateway which let you vomit dice at your opponent. Nine is still pretty good, but now you might as well start using em once you hit that number.

Small change to Flamers as well, their persistent burning ability didn't work when in reserves. Since it works when the unit was destroyed, it likely was intended from the start it'd work from reserve as well.

Over to points changes, leaning toward more hikes given the army's decent status. Points hike to the Ogroid Thaumaturge and both hero and base version of Chariot. Scourge of Aqshy Screamers were also way too cheap, so a slight points hike was fair. The Silver Summoner trait to summon replacement units costs points now, which is fair since it created a lot of extra value.  The Gaunt Summoners did go down, at least, and Tzaangors of all stripes remain untouched.

Verdict: Slight Loser

Hedonites of Slaanesh

I think we all saw this coming. No rules changes, but as one of the strongest books to come out in the past few months, there had to be hits on some of the stronger units. Lord of Hysteria and The Masque both went up 20 points and Thricefold Discord and Painbringers went up 10. For the Painbringers this is especially rough, since it was common to run 3 reinforced units of them. That said, there were a few cuts; Daemonettes went down 10 (and I think they're better than they're given credit for). The twins, Keeper of Secrets and Lord of Pain went down in points, so overall it may open up some new play options.

Surprisingly, Shalaxi was left untouched, which is nice.

Verdict: Loser

Helsmiths of Hashut

Helsmiths got a huge overhaul. The biggest issue with the Helsmiths right now is basically that everyone is using an Army of Renown and not the actual army. So all four battle traits in the main army were rewritten. The general gist is that all the previous battle traits required 3 Demonic Power Points on a unit to activate their ability. This is a huge investment that won't be useful until probably the second round of the game (And that's committing basically all your resources to one unit).

The new versions scale better. Amassed Legions now only requires 1 DPP and the benefit doesn't apply to just infantry, as long as the infantry unit has the DPP, anyone within 3" can benefit, very solid. Arcane Dominance gives +1 to cast/chant/unbind to all Wizards and Priests within 12" of another Wizard or Priest with a single DPP. A bit convoluted to set up but if two of them have a DPP, then every caster in your army can get the buff. Bulls of the Ziggurat gives +1" of movement for each DPP now instead of 2" for 3 for only specific units. Probably the best, especially now that it affects everyone. Castigation Battery gives Crit (2 Hits) to ranged weapons with 2 DPP. Probably the least exciting, and possibly worse than before unless you spike well.

Are these worth it? Eh, hard to say. I like them, for the most part. The issue is the army take so long to rev up that by the time you have enough DPP to do anything, games over. Tarr's Grand Forgehost gives stronger buffs off the bat, without needing to fiddle with currency.

On top of that, though, you also get some nice point drops across the board. Daemonsmith on Infernal Taurus and both Dominator Engines got a drop, both very usable units. Foot casters are, as expected, able to be included as sub commanders. So pretty solid all around.

Verdict: Winner

Maggotkin of Nurgle

Just some cuts on stuff people weren't really using. Point drops on Morbidex and Orghotts is potentially nice but the best changes are the Rotbringer Sorcerer being a subcommander for many popular heroes, and the Rotmire Creed is now reinforceable, making them a bit more scary.

Verdict: Winner

Skaven

Pretty solid gains here. Rat Ogors have been feeling the hurt since the Scourge of Ghyran Brood Horror left them behind, so they got a nice little drop to make up for it, alongside the vanilla Brood Horror. Huge 30 point drops on the Verminlord Deceiver and Screech the Vermin King also feel pretty nice as these are arguably the best Verminlord builds for the kit.

The most exciting change is for Krittok Foulblade who no longer has to pay a CP for his ability to use Three Clawsteps Ahead on two units. Maybe not an auto include, but that's a big buff if you have any important Verminus units. Warlock Galvaneer also no longer requires a die roll, since a 2+ on a Once Per Battle ability can hurt pretty badly.

Verdict: Winner

Slaves to Darkness

Brand of the Unaligned can no longer be used on a unit with an Ensorcelled Banner, to prevent weirdness with being able to change mark but keep the banner. While I don't think this was excessively broken, I understand how it went against the spirit of the rules.

In exchange, a fair number of points drops. Abraxia, Archaeon and Varanguard drops will likely be appreciated, along with a scattering of a few less-used units like the Vortex Beast/Slaughterbrute, Furies and Chaos Lord on Karkadrak.

Chaos Sorcerer Lord being a subcommander is pretty sweet now, as is the fact that Chaos Warriors and Chosen remained untouched.

Verdict: Winner

Death

Flesh-eater Courts

A fair number of drops, mostly on unused heroes. Crypt Horrors and Crypt Ghouls dropping is pretty nice. GW seems to want to push the infantry side a lot harder now that they sufficiently nerfed Terrorgheists.

Royal Beastflayers did go up, but they can be reinforced now, and I think they're one of the units you would possibly look into doing that for, so that's nice.

Verdict: Winner

Nighthaunt

Nighthaunt were beneficiaries of some big warscroll changes this updated. Death Stalkers, a not often used subfaction has gone from Retreat and Shoot/Charge (an effect they can access quite easily otherwise) to -1 Rend against a unit of your choice. Once you kill that unit, you get to pick a new one, which is nice. Nighthaunt lack real strong offensive options so this is a nice little perk for them. It's also surprising to see the change be so radical, as it is unrecognizable from the old version.

The Shadowy Aura went from a -1 to be hit when Redeploying (A very niche situation) to a 9" hidden aura for Infantry and Cav. That is a huge buff and maybe not as good as Ruler of the Spectral Hosts (which is free now, by the way), still pretty damn good.

For the Scriptor Mortis, the Sentenced to Eternal Torment ability is now for the rest of the game instead of the end of turn. Less clumsy sure, but I think I would have preferred to remove the 3+ (Or give a way to get around it).

Speaking of ways around a 3+, the Lord Vitriolic's Spectral Alchemy also got shaken up. Instead of on a 3+ for picking one effect or rolling two dice at random, you either get one of your choice on a 3+ or if you did any damage with the ranged attack, get it for free. While not getting two seems like a downside, a way to circumvent the 3+ is huge and you almost never took the roll for 2 ability. Was it fun? Sure, but so many of the effects were extremely niche and you risked rolling something like shut off wards on a thing without wards. It's for the best.

GW hit the emergency "Faction is in trouble" button here. They removed the cost of all the upgrades, and gave some points drops to unused unit like the Scriptor Mortis above. Pyregheists also can now be reinforced, which seems like a pretty good play if you still run these guys. Didn't even go up in points either.

Verdict: Significant Winner

Ossiarch Bonereapers

Huge win here. Ossiarchs are currently at the very bottom and so Games Workshop has hit the emergency "reduce the cost of everything" button. I mean just about everything was dropped with Necropolis Stalkers, Immortis Guard and Morghast (both kinds) being some of the big winners. Discounts on some of the bigger models like Katakros, Arkhan and Nagash as well.

There's a pretty big rules change, too. Relentless Discipline used to scale up, with reinforced units costing 2 RDP instead of 1. This also applies to  Katakros's warscroll relentless discipline as well. While it probably doesn't salvage his Warscroll ability, since the cost came from using high wound units (where you'd want to use that ability anyway) it's huge for the rest of the army. Bringing large hammer units like Morghast or reinforced Stalkers was a huge liability as they'd eat through your RDP very quickly. This may move the meter back toward more high damage unit instead of the Deathrider charge and retreat strat that the army has come to rely on.

As a small perk, all the functionally similar wizards being able to be a sub-commander is nice and may help them see a bit more play.

Verdict: Winner

Soulblight Gravelords

The Aqshy Vengorian Lordwas a bit overtuned, able to move D3+Fury Level Inches in the combat phase. The D3 has been removed and the ability is in the charge phase instead. This likely exists to prevent combat phase abilities that target an enemy unit to then effectively fizzle out when the Vengorian Lord moves right after, but the reduction in inches is the big change. Still powerful, probably still worth taking.

Some pretty big changes for points, both up and down. Askurgan Trueblades did go up by 10, but they can be reinforced now. They're probably the biggest beneficiaries of this change across the whole game, especially if you want to run Prince Vhordrai, who did come down in points. As did Blood Knights and Vampire Lord on Steed so a true Vampire list may be workable again.

The Aqshy exclusive buff The Never-dead was given a 10 point hike to 20 pts. A popular take on reinforced Deadwalkers, giving them a 5+ Invul save since those didn't go up, you'll probably still see this as it's a powerful combo.

Overall, pretty good changes, didn't hit anything crucial too bad and it's quite workable if you want to keep building to the previous meta

Verdict: Winner

Destruction

Gloomspite Gitz

Kind of a baffling set of changes here; Sunsteala Wheelaz and the War Wheelz heroes went down. Snarlpack Cavalry is probably the best decrease here, since we haven't seen those in a minute. Then the Scourge of Aqshy stuff went down.

Just...nothing exciting here. No new sub-commanders, not even a Warcry Warband to talk about.

Verdict: Yawn

Ironjawz

Gordrakk and both Megabosses went down. So cheaper cabbages, but the catch is you're paying +10 more for Brutez. GW seems to want to encourage you to use anything else, which I don't think is a hard sell. With Warchanter and Weirdnob Shaman available as sub commanders now, you can condense the list down a bit and make up for it.

Verdict: Winner

Kruleboyz

Shockingly, Kruleboyz have been mostly left alone. They tend to get swatted down once they start doing good, but GW seems to have taken a softer hand here. Some points reductions to the Killaboss with Stab Grot and Hobgrot Slittaboss. Monsta-Killas went up, but again, can be reinforced now which you might actually want to do.

Being able to put the Swampcalla Shaman in a regiment with one of the bigger boys is possibly useful, since it's basically your requisite wizard if you're not running Gobsprakk.

Verdict: Winner

Ogor Mawtribes

Ogors haven't been out that long with their new book, and everyone agrees they do not like Redd the Maw and Gluttons. Redd gives Gluttons their 6+ Ward, and the Gluttons themselves were far too cheap for how many wounds they get to have. Their save isn't even bad, able to rock a 4+ save. So they had to go up for sure. Hunters on Sabrefangs, the other popular unit in the few lists we've seen also went up.

A few random other units went down, probably to compensate and recommend more diverse listbuilding. These sorts of small tweaks aren't unusual in a new book as they both want to let things settle a bit but also be proactive with things that are wildly powerful.

Verdict: Loser

Sons of Behemat

Since the book is coming out very soon, they're not gonna make major changes. The changes here are largely maintenance. Due to the massive overhaul to the fundamental design of the models, a lot of currently existing content that is technically legal but clashes with the rules of the new book needed to be updated and now was the best time to do it.

Most of it is boring bookkeeping stuff, Mega-Gargant is word-replaced with Big, and Gargant is Word-Replaced with Little where relevant. Probably the biggest question was what was going to happen to the Aqshy Gatebreaker since it uses the old profile for a Gatebreaker. Naturally the answer was just to rewrite it to match the new one. 25 wounds, 10 control, and the new combat profile.

King Brodd's Stomp Army of Renown will remain legal, but it was updated to match the new book. As mentioned above, Mega-Gargants are now Bigs, and Gargants are now Littles. Rampages are "Destructive Impulse" and any removed abilities like Almightier Stomp are removed. It's difficult to say if it'll still be worth it with the new book, but it's at least still usable.

The last change is kinda surprising, the Grotmas Stumblefoot Gargant Regiment of Renown was removed, a first for the game. On the other hand, the new Tome has its own Regiment of Renown that's a single little Gargant, so there's not much reason for it to exist. So in the bin it goes, better with updated language.

Points didn't change at all, since they just got dropped so kinda pointless to change right now.

Verdict: Bookkeeping

Wrap Up

Honestly, a bigger change than I expected. The last change was massive, which was expected with the dawn of a new season. This of course wasn't going to quite live up to that, but it's still a lot of changes.

Games Workshop seems a lot more willing to directly tackle warscrolls and battle traits and do top to bottom rewrites if they need to. This is big for the state of the game, especially since many early Battletomes for the edition are a bit lackluster or to put it simply, boring.

I think these changes are going to be positive for the flow of the game, especially the armies that are struggling more. It's a harder read on the armies that are doing very well and needed a nerf, but it's a lot better to raise up the floor than lower the ceiling, unless the circumstances are very extreme.
